title: Sound & Tones
description: A piano Rich Losey and I wrote that knows key signatures. Pick a key, and each letter key plays the note that key calls for. Dated 10-14-82.
versionOrder: Disk saves have no recorded order or dates beyond their source comments. Any ordering here is a presentation guess.

versions.label: Sound & Tones (blocks 80-84)
versions.note: Source blocks copied unchanged from the New Programs disk. The player boots the Forth System disk and loads them with the original commands. Checked to its first screen only. Key signatures, accidentals, and the base-17 printout were checked in the emulator; pitch accuracy has not been judged by ear.

attribution.text: Rich Losey and I wrote this together; he is my friend and was my roommate. It runs on MMSFORTH V2.0, © 1981 Miller Microcomputer Services. Preserved here for small-scale archival use.

howTo: What this is: a piano that reads like sheet music. In the key of F, every B is B-flat, so you press the B key and hear B-flat, just as a musician does. The program holds a table of which notes each key makes sharp or flat, and it applies that table to every key you press.

To play: click the screen, type KEYBOARD, and press Enter. Then choose a key with a button below: A♭, B♭, C, D, E♭, F, G, or A. Choose one first. Until you do, the tables are empty and every key plays its sharp.

The letter rows are the piano. Each row runs A, B, C, D, E, F, G from the left, and keys past G continue into the next octave. The Z row is highest, then A, then Q. The number row is mostly a placeholder pitch. A note sounds only while you hold its key.
Accidentals: hold ↑ or Enter with a note to sharpen it, or ↓ or Space to flatten it. In the key of C, ↑ with B gives C, and ↓ with B gives B-flat.

The printout shows each note in base 17. An octave has 17 slots: the sharps first, then A through G in slots 10 to 16. Base 17 writes those slots as the digits A through G, so a natural note prints under its own name. 1C is C in octave 1, and 10 is the first slot in that octave, the one for B-flat and A-sharp.

How it makes sound: there is no sound chip. A short loop flips the cassette port on and off, and a table named TUNEFISH holds the delay for each note. Hold ← or → with a note to retune it by ear; the program prints the note’s new delay after IS NOW. The change lasts until you restart.

The other two keyboards: type DELTABOARD for an experiment where each key moves relative to the last note, or OLDBOARD for the simple board used for demos. KEYBOARD and DELTABOARD run until you press Restart.
quickHelp: Type KEYBOARD, press Enter, and choose a key below. Letter rows play notes while held. ↑ sharpens, ↓ flattens, and ← → retune.
